name: Amazon EC2 on-demand virtual computation
description: A network service rented virtual compute capacity that developers could configure for their own applications.

impact.note: A tool for software developers and firms; deployment of software was reorganised around rented capacity, and the cloud computing line grew from it.

date.label: 25 August 2006
date.basis: Date or stated historical interval in cited source; see caveats.

events.statement: Amazon described EC2 as open to limited beta testing at an hourly compute charge.

contributions.resource: Supplied the beta virtual computing service.

evidence.supports: AWS describes a limited beta and 10 cents per clock hour.

events.caveats: Limited beta availability was not universal access; networking and storage costs are not included in the compute price.

evidence.supports: AWS describes a limited beta and 10 cents per clock hour.

date.label: 22 October 2007
date.basis: Date or stated historical interval in cited source; see caveats.

events.statement: AWS announced that its EC2 beta was open for all developers to sign up.
events.caveats: Open signup does not imply free use or prove participation by any user.

earliest_record.rationale: Earliest sourced event establishing this scoped achievement; it is not a claim of global priority.

measures.unit: USD per virtual CPU clock hour
measures.money_context: Nominal 2006 beta rate; excludes other service charges.
measures.subject: Original EC2 virtual CPU
measures.conditions: AWS blog says 10 cents per clock hour; one original virtual CPU configuration, limited beta.

evidence.supports: Provider states 10 cents per clock hour.

caveats: Earlier time-sharing, hosting and utility-computing services existed. EC2 was one commercial infrastructure service, not the invention of remote computing.

research.note: New source-backed draft; independent review pending. Independent reader checked AWS’s limited 2006 beta, configuration and clock-hour price and its 2007 broader beta announcement.
